## Paired t-tests

A **paired t-test** is used when two measurements are taken on the *same* subjects (e.g., before and after treatment), rather than on two independent groups. Instead of comparing two separate samples, we compute the **difference** for each subject and run a one-sample t-test on those differences, testing whether the average difference is 0.

**Conditions:**

- Random sample of pairs/subjects
- Independent pairs (the differences themselves are independent across subjects)
- $n > 30$, __or__ the differences follow a normal distribution in the population

$$H_0: \mu_d = 0 \qquad \text{vs.} \qquad H_A: \mu_d \ne 0 \ \ (\text{or} \ <, \ >)$$

where $\mu_d$ is the population mean of the paired differences.

In our hypertension trial, each patient has both a baseline and a follow-up SBP measurement&mdash;the same patient, measured twice. That makes `sbp_change` (follow-up minus baseline) a natural candidate for a paired analysis: __did SBP change significantly from baseline to follow-up, within each treatment group?__

### Drug A: Test by Hand

We will now calculate the test statistic for the Drug A group:

```{code-blanks-instructions}
Fill in the code below to calculate the test statistic for a paired t-test on the Drug A group's change scores.
```

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|   target: diff_a
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 3
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: sd_a
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 3
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: n_a
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 3
#|   match: token

# Drug A summary statistics
diff_a = mean(data_a$sbp_change)
sd_a = sd(data_a$sbp_change)
n_a = nrow(data_a)

# print values
diff_a ; sd_a ; n_a

# test statistic
t_a = diff_a / (sd_a / sqrt(n_a))
t_a
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

``` r
# Drug A summary statistics
diff_a = mean(data_a$sbp_change)
sd_a = sd(data_a$sbp_change)
n_a = nrow(data_a)

# print values
diff_a ; sd_a ; n_a

# test statistic
t_a = diff_a / (sd_a / sqrt(n_a))
t_a
```
[[1] -10.0667]{style="font-family: 'Monaco'; font-weight: 500; font-size : 12px;"}

This is an __extremely large__ test statistic in magnitude, suggesting very strong evidence that SBP decreased from baseline to follow-up in the Drug A group.
:::

```{code-blanks-instructions}
Now calculate the two-sided p-value and a 95% confidence interval for the mean change.
```

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|   target: n_a - 1
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: 0.025
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: 0.975
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: n_a - 1
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 2
#|   match: token

# two-sided p-value
2 * pt(abs(t_a), df = n_a - 1, lower.tail = F)

# 95% confidence interval
diff_a + qt(c(0.025, 0.975), df = n_a - 1) * (sd_a / sqrt(n_a))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

``` r
# two-sided p-value
2 * pt(abs(t_a), df = n_a - 1, lower.tail = F)
```
[[1] 7.825647e-17]{style="font-family: 'Monaco'; font-weight: 500; font-size : 12px;"}
``` r
# 95% confidence interval
diff_a + qt(c(0.025, 0.975), df = n_a - 1) * (sd_a / sqrt(n_a))
```
[[1] -12.950227  -8.685646]]{style="font-family: 'Monaco'; font-weight: 500; font-size : 12px;"}

The p-value very small, and the 95% CI (-12.95, -8.69) is entirely below 0&mdash;strong evidence of a real decrease in SBP for the Drug A group.
:::

### Drug A: Test with `t.test()`

```{code-blanks-instructions}
Fill in the code below to run a paired t-test using `t.test()`. There are two equivalent ways to do this: running a one-sample test directly on the `sbp_change` column, or passing the original `sbp_followup` and `sbp_baseline` columns with `paired = T`. Try the second approach here.
```

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|   target: sbp_followup
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1

#|   prefill: false

#|   match: token

# paired t-test (Drug A)
t.test(x = data_a$sbp_followup, y = data_a$sbp_baseline, paired = T)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

``` r
# paired t-test (Drug A)
t.test(x = data_a$sbp_followup, y = data_a$sbp_baseline, paired = T)
```

This should give (approximately) the same test statistic, p-value, and conclusion as our hand calculation above. Try also running `t.test(data_a$sbp_change)` as a one-sample test&mdash;you should get identical results, since a paired t-test *is* just a one-sample t-test on the differences.
:::

### What If We Didn't Pair?

It's important to use a paired test when data are paired! Let's see what happens if we (incorrectly) run an unpaired (independent samples) t-test on the same baseline and follow-up values for the Drug A group.

```{code-blanks-instructions}
Fill in the code below to run the __incorrect__, unpaired version of the test on the Drug A group's baseline and follow-up values (`paired = F`), for comparison.
```

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|   target: sbp_followup
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: sbp_baseline
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: F
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token

# INCORRECT: unpaired test on the same (paired) data
t.test(x = data_a$sbp_followup, y = data_a$sbp_baseline, paired = F)
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

``` r
# INCORRECT: unpaired test on the same (paired) data
t.test(x = data_a$sbp_followup, y = data_a$sbp_baseline, paired = F)
```

The test statistic here is __smaller in magnitude__ than our paired version, even though we're using the exact same data! That's because the unpaired test ignores the fact that baseline and follow-up measurements come from the *same* patients, and so it fails to account for (and remove) the variability between patients&mdash;variability that the paired test cancels out by looking at within-patient differences.
:::

```{code-blanks-response}
Based on what you just saw, why does using the wrong (unpaired) test when data are actually paired tend to make it *harder* to detect a real effect, rather than easier?
```

## Power and Sample Size for Paired t-tests

Power and sample size calculations for a paired t-test work exactly like the one-sample case, using the standard deviation of the *differences*.

```{code-blanks-instructions}
Suppose we want to detect a mean difference (`delta`) of __2 mmHg__, assuming a standard deviation of the differences of __10__, with a significance level of __0.05__ and __80% power__, using a __one-sided__ test. Fill in the code below to find the required sample size.
```

```{code-blanks}
#| blank:
#|   target: 2
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: 10
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: 0.05
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: 0.8
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: "one.sample"
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token
#| blank:
#|   target: "one.sided"
#|   prefill: false
#|   occurrence: 1
#|   match: token

# required sample size for 80% power
power.t.test(delta = 2, 
             sd = 10, 
             sig.level = 0.05, 
             power = 0.8,
             type = "one.sample", 
             alternative = "one.sided")
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

``` r
# required sample size for 80% power
power.t.test(delta = 2, 
             sd = 10, 
             sig.level = 0.05, 
             power = 0.8,
             type = "one.sample", 
             alternative = "one.sided")
```

[n = 155.9257]{style="font-family: 'Monaco'; font-weight: 500; font-size : 12px;"}

We'd need about __156 patients__ to reliably detect a mean difference of 2 mmHg given this much variability in the differences.
:::

```{code-blanks-response}
Our actual Drug A group only has n = 100 patients. Using `power.t.test()` with `n = 100` instead of solving for sample size, what power do we actually have to detect a 2 mmHg difference? Is it above or below 80%? (You should get something close to 63%.)
```
